## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/mcp-server-for-project-plan.html

Answer

# Is there an MCP server for a project plan?

Yes — KaidoPlan has one built in. 21 tools over stdio or a loopback endpoint, covering tasks, dependencies, resources, baselines, scheduling and violation checks. Every write tool persists on its own; there is no save step to forget.

Updated 2026-11-17 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What MCP actually buys over parsing the file

The plan is already plain JSON, so an agent could read it with `cat` and write it with a text editor. That works for reading and is a bad idea for writing, for three reasons that have nothing to do with convenience:

- Writing a consistent document is harder than reading one. A status change also moves the project's `updatedAt`, may need to record a completion time, and may invalidate dates downstream. Hand-editing JSON gets the field right and the consequences wrong.

- A tool call can fail loudly. `task_update` with an unknown identifier returns an error. A careful string edit with the wrong UUID returns a file that parses perfectly and contains a dependency pointing at nothing.

- Some answers are computed, not stored. The critical path is not a field in the file. An agent reading the JSON can see durations and edges and still get the chain wrong — the schedule engine cannot, because it is the thing the app's Gantt chart also calls.

That last point is the design constraint worth stating: the CLI, the MCP server and the window are the same engine. A command-line answer and the highlighted chain in the chart cannot disagree, because there is one implementation.

## The 21 tools

Group

Tools

What it is for

Project

`project_create`, `project_open`, `project_save`

Open a plan, create one, save as

Tasks and WBS

`task_add`, `task_list`, `task_get`, `task_update`, `task_delete`, `wbs_import`

Read and change the structure, including edges and constraints

Scheduling

`schedule_compute`, `schedule_critical_path`

Turn dependencies into dates and slack

Violations

`violations_list`

Cycles, deadline conflicts, dates outside the project window

Write-back

`status_update`, `status_batch_update`

Record progress and completion times

Resources

`resource_add`, `resource_list`

People, equipment, materials

Baselines

`baseline_create`, `baseline_list`, `baseline_delete`, `baseline_variance`, `baseline_set_color`

Freeze a schedule, then compare plan against actuals

Client setup is one switch per client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy — and the switch writes only the `mcpServers.kaidoplan` key into that client's configuration, leaving the rest of the file byte-identical. The app binary can also run as a stdio server directly (`--mcp-stdio`), so a client can start it without a separate CLI install.

## A session, end to end

What the tool surface looks like when an agent is actually working. Four calls, in this order, and the fourth is the one that is always skipped:

- `project_open` with the file path. Returns `formatVersion` and whether the file will be upgraded on the next save — worth reading before you let an older client write to a newer plan.

- `task_list` filtered by parent, or `project_summary`'s CLI equivalent for the aggregate. This is the read that replaces the recap paragraph.

- `status_batch_update` with an array of task IDs, statuses and progress. Returns per-entry success and failure: one bad identifier rejects that entry and leaves the rest applied, so a partial write is visible rather than silent.

- `schedule_compute`, then `violations_list`. The recompute is what turns "I marked it done" into "the date is still valid, or it is not".

Every write tool persists to disk on its own. `project_save` exists for explicit saves, save-as, and retrying after a `saved:false` result — it is not a step the agent has to remember in the normal loop.

## The security model, in three lines

- Loopback only: the endpoint listens on `127.0.0.1`, never the LAN or the internet.

- Every request carries a token the app generates locally and shows in its panel.

- Only folders you authorised in that panel are reachable; anything else is refused, before the file is opened.

The server is on by default since v3.4.0, on the loopback address with a token. Turning it off in the panel stops access immediately, and a previous explicit off setting is not overridden by that default change.

## Read versus write

Reading a plan through the server — listing tasks, computing the schedule, listing violations — needs no licence at all. Writing status, actual dates, edges or new tasks back into the plan requires a Pro entitlement, which the 30-day trial grants in full. The split is not arbitrary: the write tools are the operations that can move a delivery date. An agent that can silently rewrite edges can silently rewrite the answer you report to a client.

If you would rather not add an MCP client at all, the CLI exposes the same operations from a shell, and the file is readable JSON. Nothing about the workflow depends on MCP; it is one of three ways in.

## What it does not do

- No remote access. The endpoint is loopback-only by design, so the agent has to run on the same Mac. A hosted agent cannot reach it, and that is the trade for not having an authentication story to get wrong.

- No multi-user coordination. Two agents writing at once is two writers on one file; the last save wins, including its stale view of everything it did not touch. Serialise the writers.

- No partial-file access. There is no "give the agent only task 12". It gets the plan it opened, which is why the folder authorisation list matters more than the token.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it work with a remote or hosted agent?

No. The endpoint is loopback-only by design, so the agent has to run on the same Mac.

Is the server on by default?

Yes since v3.4.0, on 127.0.0.1 with a token. Turning it off in the panel stops access immediately; a previous explicit off setting is not overridden by the default change.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/why-ai-projects-miss-deadlines.html

QA

# AI-assisted projects miss deadlines — and the arithmetic that catches it

Every task says done. The agent's summary says done. The pull requests are merged. And the delivery date has moved anyway.

Updated 2026-11-09 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## "Done" is a property of a task. The delivery date is a property of a graph.

This is the most common failure in AI-assisted projects, and it is almost never a coding failure. Nobody lied, nobody slacked off, and no story was misreported. The status report and the schedule are describing two different objects, and they were never required to agree.

A task can be genuinely, verifiably complete and still ruin the date, because the date is produced by a chain of predecessors — and a chain does not care how green its individual nodes are.

### Failure 1: the finished task that finished too late

Agents execute in the order they are asked, which is not always the order the plan implies.

Suppose server work finishes on the 6th, and client integration began on the 4th. Both statements can be true. Nothing in a task list objects, because a task list has no concept of one task having to precede another. A schedule does: it reports the pair as a date conflict, and it does so on the 4th, not on the 20th when someone asks for a date.

This is the single most valuable property of putting dates and edges in the same object. The contradiction becomes an error message instead of a surprise in a client call.

### Failure 2: the dependency was never written down

Most plans record tasks and dates and stop there. Without an edge between two tasks, the data model has no way to express "the acceptance test cannot start before the API exists."

So the schedule compresses. The computed finish date comes out earlier than reality, the plan looks healthy, and it keeps looking healthy right up to the week the gap becomes undeniable. The information was never missing from the project — it was missing from the artifact.

A useful test for any tracker: can you express "B cannot start until A finishes" such that a machine will complain when that is violated? If the answer is "we agreed on that in Slack," you have a plan that cannot be checked.

### Failure 3: the estimate was never yours

Ask an agent how long a task will take and you get an average case, with no memory of the last time this class of task went wrong. The agent is not being optimistic on purpose; it has no prior to be pessimistic with.

Across a plan of forty tasks, that bias does not average out. It compounds, because every task inherits the same missing memory. Speed then makes the outcome worse, not better: the work arrives faster, the slip arrives just as fast, and it is more surprising because everything felt productive.

The division of labour that survives contact with reality is boring: the agent writes the code, the person who has shipped before sets the duration. Not because humans estimate well, but because a human estimate carries the memory of previous failures and can be argued with in review.

### Failure 4: integration, review and acceptance get estimated at zero

They are where schedule compression goes to hide. They also feel like formalities, so they get zero days — or they get dropped entirely because "the tasks are the work."

A plan without them looks a week shorter and is a week wrong. If your plan has no explicit task for review and acceptance, you have not omitted overhead; you have moved it into the part of the timeline nobody is measuring.

### Failure 5: you are watching the wrong tasks

A daily report over forty green tasks trains everyone to look at volume. But the delivery date is set by the zero-slack chain — usually two or three tasks, and rarely the ones discussed in standup.

This is why status meetings feel productive and move nothing. Optimising the visible set is satisfying; only the critical path changes the date. If you cannot name the chain that sets your end date, you are managing a list, not a schedule.

## A worked example

Four tasks, dates included, small enough to check by hand:

Task

Dates

Status

API design

ends Nov 1

done

Server implementation

ends Nov 6

done

Client integration

starts Nov 4; predecessor ends Nov 7

date conflict

Joint acceptance

critical path, 0 days slack

blocks the end date

Three of four tasks are green. Two problems are visible in the table and invisible in a status report:

- Client integration starts on Nov 4 against a predecessor that ends Nov 7 — three days of work running before the thing it depends on exists.

- Joint acceptance sits on the zero-slack chain. Any day it moves, the delivery date moves one-for-one.

Neither is a coding error. Both are arithmetic errors in the plan, and both are cheap to fix on Nov 4 and expensive to explain on Nov 20.

## The check that catches all five

You do not need a methodology. You need four operations run against the plan data after every change that touches dates:

`# 1. Does the schedule compute at all? Early/late dates per task.
kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido

# 2. Which chain sets the end date? Critical path and slack.
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido

# 3. What does the plan admit is broken?
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido

# 4. Did the agent's status write-back actually land?
kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido --json`

Step 3 returns four classes of problem, and each has exactly one honest response:

Violation

What it means

What to do

Dependency cycle

A waits for B and B waits for A

Break the cycle. Nothing downstream is real.

Deadline conflict

A task finishes after a constraint or the project end

Move the date, cut scope, or move the constraint — decide deliberately

Task outside the project window

Starts before the project starts or ends after it ends

Either the window is wrong or the task belongs elsewhere

Blocked chain

Work that cannot proceed because an upstream item is stuck

Escalate this chain today, not the loudest task in the list

The result you are looking for is boring: no violations, and a critical path you can name out loud. If you cannot say which chain sets your date, the check has not been done — it has been performed.

One detail worth internalising: bulk status writes should return per-entry success and failure, and they should not abort on the first failure. That is correct behaviour for a long list, and it is exactly why you have to read the output. Nine of ten entries landing looks like success from a distance.

## Make it a failing test, not a ritual

A schedule check that lives in a weekly meeting decays into ritual within a month. A schedule check that lives in CI does not.

If the plan is a file in the repository, the check can be part of the pull request you were going to open anyway: run `violations`, paste the output, and if it is non-empty the change is not ready. No dashboard, no webhook, no account. When it passes it costs nothing, and when it fails you learn about a dependency cycle at commit time instead of at delivery time.

The same reasoning applies to the "done" definition. Make done mean done, and the plan recomputed — not as a slogan, but as the literal gate. Writing status through the tool surface rather than in prose matters here, because the completion time is what a conflict check needs; "done" as a boolean is enough for a burndown and useless for a schedule.

## What none of this fixes

This check does not shorten your critical path. It tells you which chain sets the date so you can decide what to cut, parallelise, or renegotiate. The decision stays with you.

It does not fix a bad estimate either — a plan can be internally consistent and still unachievable. Consistency is the cheap half: it is the only half you can compute.

And it does not replace a project manager, a standup, or a conversation with a client. It makes the slip visible on the day it happens instead of the week it becomes undeniable, which is the only window in which a deadline can still be protected.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does the tool shorten the critical path?

No. It tells you which chain sets the date so you can decide what to cut or parallelise. The decision stays yours.

Is this a scheduling problem or a communication problem?

Both, but the scheduling error is the one that cannot be argued with. That is why it is worth computing first.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/export-delivery-report.html

Answer

# How do I export a delivery report for a client?

A delivery report is not a screenshot of a task list. It is an argument with four parts, and every number in it should be reproducible from the plan file the client can be handed.

Updated 2026-11-17 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Four sections, in this order

Order matters because each section depends on the one before it. A report that opens with percentages has already lost the argument.

- The computed finish date. Not the date someone hoped for, and not a range invented for safety. The number the schedule produces from the current durations and edges.

- The chain that produces it. The critical path, named by task. This is the load-bearing section: it converts "trust me" into "these three tasks decide the date, and here they are".

- Open violations. Conflicts, cycles, tasks outside the project window. A report that hides an open conflict is a report that will be contradicted next week, by the person who reads the plan themselves.

- Variance against a baseline. Planned versus actual per milestone, so that "on track" is a measurement rather than an adjective.

## What a section 1–4 report looks like

Milestone

Baseline finish

Computed finish

Variance

Import pipeline accepted

2026-11-21

2026-11-21

0 days

Reconciliation report signed off

2026-11-27

2026-11-28

+1 day

Handover to operations

2026-12-04

2026-12-08

+4 days

Then the sentence that makes the table useful: "The four days are on the reconciliation chain — the fixture set took a day longer than planned, and the handover rehearsal is serialised behind it." That is a report. The table alone is a spreadsheet, and the percentage-complete column that usually accompanies it says nothing about the date.

Note what the middle row does to the last: a one-day slip upstream becomes four days at the end, because the tasks after it have no slack. This is the single most common thing a client does not believe until they see the chain.

## Where each number comes from

Every figure in the report is one command away, which is what makes it auditable rather than asserted:

Report line

Command

Computed finish date

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido`

The deciding chain, with slack

`kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

Open violations

`kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

Variance per milestone

`kaidoplan baseline variance --baseline <id> --file plan.kaido`

The same variance as data

`kaidoplan baseline variance --baseline <id> --csv variance.csv --file plan.kaido`

The `--csv` form is the one worth knowing about if the client wants the numbers in their own tracker: it writes the per-task variance rows to a file instead of printing them, and the project-level totals stay identical to what the report shows.

## Preview before you send

If you want the habit before the report, the five-minute delivery check is the same four numbers in a smaller loop. The app's workbench previews the delivery report before export, which is the cheapest place to catch a number that contradicts the text you wrote around it. Export is unlimited during the trial; on the free tier it is three reports a month, with the rest of the planning workbench intact.

## The baseline habit that makes reports cheap

Take a baseline at the start of each reporting period — `kaidoplan baseline create --name "Sprint 12 start" --file plan.kaido`. From then on the report is a comparison, not a narrative written from memory.

It also removes the most common argument in a delivery review: whether the date changed or was always wrong. With a baseline the question has a diff answer. Without one, both sides are describing their recollection of a document, and the person who is more senior usually wins.

Two rules for baselines, learned the hard way:

- Baseline after you accept a change, not before. A baseline taken mid-negotiation freezes a schedule nobody agreed to.

- Keep them. A baseline you deleted is a variance you cannot compute, and the period it covered becomes unauditable retroactively.

## What to leave out

- Percentage complete, as a headline. Forty tasks at 70% tells the reader nothing about the date, and it invites the question "so are we on track", which is the question the report exists to answer without being asked.

- Task counts. "38 of 52 done" is a volume metric. The date is set by the zero-slack chain, which is usually two or three tasks.

- Any number you cannot reproduce. If a figure in the report does not come from a command in the plan, it is a claim wearing a table's clothing, and the first technical reader will find it.

## When the number is bad

The report is most valuable on the week the date moves, and that is the week people rewrite it. The structure that survives a bad number is the same structure as always, with one added paragraph at the top:

The delivery date is now 8 December, four days later than the baseline of 4 December. The change is on the reconciliation chain: the fixture set took a day longer, and the handover rehearsal is serialised behind it. To recover the four days, either the rehearsal moves in parallel with sign-off, or the fixture scope drops to the two formats that matter.

Date, cause, options. No apology and no optimism. A client who receives that in week two trusts the next report; a client who receives "still on track" for six weeks and then a four-week slip does not, and the arithmetic was available the whole time.

Keep the plan in the repository and the report has a source you can point at — a commit, a baseline and a diff. That is a stronger position than a slide deck nobody can audit, and it is the difference between reporting a schedule and defending one.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I export to PDF or CSV?

The app's delivery report export is the supported path. The plan file is plain JSON, so any other format is a short script away if you need one.

Can I export reports during the free trial?

Yes. The trial includes unlimited delivery-report exports.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/project-files.html

Features · 3 tools

# The plan is a file, not an account

Three tools, one object: a `.kaido` file you can copy, diff, back up and read without the app.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The three tools

Tool

Does

`project_create`

Creates a project. Optional `projectStart` / `projectEnd` (ISO 8601) set the window that scheduling and violation checks are measured against.

`project_open`

Opens a `.kaido` file. Reports `formatVersion` and whether a save would upgrade the file.

`project_save`

Saves to the open file, or acts as save-as when a path is given.

## Why the format matters

The plan is plain JSON with a `formatVersion` field, currently 2. That single decision carries most of the properties people actually want:

- It goes in the repository. Next to the code, reviewed in the same pull request, with one-line diffs when a date moves.

- It outlives the tool. If this app disappears tomorrow, the plan is still a JSON document with a documented shape.

- It is inspectable without permission. An agent, a script or a person with `jq` can read it. No export step, no API key.

- It is local. No account, no sync, no server copy. The app's only unprompted network call is the update check.

## What "formatVersion" buys you

When the schema changes, the app knows what it is reading and upgrades on save, reporting `upgradedFrom` once so the change is visible rather than silent. Older files open; newer files are not silently rewritten.

## The project window is not metadata

Setting a start and an end date is what makes a task "outside the project window" detectable. Without a window, the violation checks have nothing to compare against, and the plan degrades into a list with dates attached.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I edit the file by hand?

It is plain JSON, so yes — and the app will load it. Keep the schema intact; the CLI and MCP tools are the safer path for structural changes.

Is there a sync service?

No. Put the file in whatever repository or backup you already trust.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/tasks-and-wbs.html

Features · 6 tools

# Tasks and the WBS

Six tools that cover the structure: create, read, filter, change, delete, and bulk import a breakdown you already have.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`task_add`

Creates a task with effort, assignee, dependencies and constraints. A constraint is written as `type:ISO8601`, e.g. `startNoLaterThan:2026-11-05T00:00:00Z`.

`task_list`

Lists tasks, optionally filtered by parent or by a natural-language filter.

`task_get`

Returns one task in full — the cheap way to check state before changing it.

`task_update`

Changes fields. Passing an empty string to `assignee` clears the owner rather than writing a blank one.

`task_delete`

Deletes a task and its subtasks, and drops dependencies that pointed at them, so no dangling edges are left behind.

`wbs_import`

Bulk-imports a nested task tree instead of retyping a breakdown that already exists.

## Structure, not fields

Groups carry hierarchy; milestones are the points where someone else has to agree; tasks carry the work, an estimate and the edges. An agent that only adds flat tasks produces a list that cannot be scheduled — which is the most common way a "generated plan" fails.

## Importing what you already have

`wbs_import` takes a nested tree and turns it into the plan. The estimate and the dependency step that follow are the ones that need a human: an imported outline with no edges schedules to a single day, and the resulting date is meaningless rather than wrong.

`kaidoplan wbs import --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan task list --file plan.kaido`

## Deletion is honest

A deleted task takes its dependencies with it. The alternative — leaving edges pointing at a task that no longer exists — produces a schedule that either fails or silently ignores the edge, and both outcomes are worse than a clean delete.

## Questions this page does not answer

Do milestones behave like zero-duration tasks?

They are the points that other tasks depend on, which is why they matter for the schedule. Treat them as checkpoints, not as work.

Can an agent rewrite the whole plan at once?

It can call the write tools in sequence. There is no bulk overwrite operation, and that is intentional: a plan replaced wholesale is a plan nobody reviewed.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/scheduling.html

Features · 2 tools

# Scheduling and the critical path

Two tools turn a dependency graph into an answer: when does this finish, and which tasks decide that.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## schedule_compute

Propagates dependencies forward and backward and returns, for every task, its earliest and latest start and finish, plus the schedule that was chosen. Forward propagation answers "when could this happen"; backward propagation answers "when must it happen without moving the end date". The gap between the two is slack, which is the number that tells you where you have room.

Constraints participate: a task with a start-no-earlier-than constraint is delayed even when its predecessor would allow an earlier start, and a finish-no-later-than constraint is what turns into a deadline conflict when the arithmetic cannot satisfy it.

## schedule_critical_path

Returns the tasks whose total slack is within a limit. With the limit at zero you get the chain that sets the finish date — usually two or three tasks, rarely the ones that dominate a status meeting.

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

## Why compute instead of tracking

A tracked date is a claim. A computed date is a consequence of the graph, and it changes when the graph changes — including when it changes for a reason nobody noticed. That is the whole value: the number moves when reality moves, not when someone remembers to update it.

Estimates remain human input. The scheduler does arithmetic on what you assert; it does not know that the last three integrations took four days instead of two.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it support resources levelling?

Resources carry units and efficiency and take part in effort conversion. Full resource-levelled scheduling is not something to assume; check what the app shows for your plan rather than trusting a page.

Can I schedule backwards from a fixed delivery date?

Yes — backward propagation is what produces latest dates, and a finish-no-later-than constraint anchors the end.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/violations.html

Features · 1 tool

# Violation checks

The plan admits what is broken, on demand, in a list you can act on.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The four classes

Violation

What it means

Dependency cycle

Two or more tasks wait on each other, so the schedule cannot be computed.

Deadline conflict

A task cannot finish by its constraint or the project end date.

Task outside the project window

Scheduled to start before the project starts or end after it ends.

Blocked chain

Work that cannot proceed because an upstream item is not moving.

## Why a list beats a warning icon

A single red indicator tells you something is wrong and nothing else. A list is actionable: each entry names the tasks involved, so the response is a decision rather than an investigation. Break the cycle, move the date, cut the scope, or accept the slip deliberately.

`kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

## In the workbench

The same checks surface in the app, inline with the plan, so a violation is visible while you are editing rather than at the end of a reporting cycle. Same data, same rules — the CLI and the app do not have separate opinions.

## The honest limitation

These are consistency checks, not feasibility checks. A plan with no violations can still be undeliverable because every estimate is optimistic. Violations tell you the arithmetic holds; only history tells you the estimates were real.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it check for resource over-allocation?

The listed classes are cycle, deadline conflict, out-of-window task and blocked chain. Do not assume more than that without checking your own plan.

Should violations block a commit?

They can, if you run the CLI in CI. Whether to block is a policy decision — a cycle almost always should.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/status-writeback.html

Features · 2 tools

# Status write-back

The difference between an agent that reports progress and one that records it: a completion time that a conflict check can use.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`status_update`

Writes status and progress for one task. Setting a task done records the completion time.

`status_batch_update`

Writes many entries at once and returns per-entry success and failure. A failing entry does not stop the remaining ones.

## Completion time is the point

"Done" as a boolean is enough for a burndown and useless for a schedule. The date a task actually finished is what determines whether the task that depended on it started too early — which is the most common real cause of a slipped date in an agent-driven project.

`kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido --json`

## Partial success looks like success

Bulk writes deliberately do not abort on the first failure. That is the right behaviour for a long list, and it means the response has to be read: nine of ten entries landing is a state you want to know about, not a state to infer.

## Write access is a paid feature

You can try AI write-back during the free trial. Continued use of write-back requires a subscription. Review schedule changes after an agent updates tasks that affect the delivery date.

## The loop to run

- The agent writes status through the tools, not through prose.

- The schedule is recomputed.

- Violations are listed.

- Any new conflict gets a decision before the next task starts.

Skip step 2 and the plan accumulates contradictions that only surface when a client asks for a date.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it save automatically?

Write operations save the session's file when there are unsaved changes, so a client does not have to call a save tool after every update.

Can I reject a write?

You control the tool surface: an agent only has the access you granted. Turning the MCP service off stops writes immediately.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/resources.html

Features · 2 tools

# Resources

A plan that says three days is making an assumption about who is doing the work. Resources make the assumption explicit.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`resource_add`

Adds a person, piece of equipment or material. `units` and `efficiency` take part in effort conversion.

`resource_list`

Lists the project's resources.

## Why bother on a solo project

Because effort and duration are not the same number. Eight hours of work is one day for one person at full attention, two days at half, and four days if the "person" is also doing support that week. Recording the resource is how the plan carries that assumption instead of hiding it in an estimate.

On an AI-assisted project the resource model also covers the non-human parts: the CI runner that can only do one build at a time, the device that has to be free for a test. Those constraints behave exactly like a busy person.

## What it does not do

Do not read this as full resource-levelled scheduling with automatic reallocation. Resources inform effort conversion and appear on the plan; the scheduler's job here is the dependency graph and the dates.

## In practice

- Add the people who will actually do the work, with realistic units.

- Record shared equipment when it is a real bottleneck.

- Re-check the critical path after a resource change: a task that becomes half-time can move the end date without any dependency changing.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I assign a task to a resource?

Tasks carry an `assignee`, which is the owner. Resources are the pool the plan describes; the two are related but not the same field.

Does efficiency affect dates?

It takes part in effort conversion, which is how duration is derived from effort — so yes, indirectly.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/baselines.html

Features · 5 tools

# Baselines and variance

Without a frozen schedule, it slipped is an opinion. A baseline turns it into two numbers.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`baseline_create`

Takes an immutable snapshot: planned start and finish plus completion state are frozen. Returns the baseline's id, name, colour and entry count.

`baseline_list`

Lists baselines in creation order, oldest first.

`baseline_variance`

Compares both the current plan and the actual dates against a baseline. Omitting the id uses the most recent one.

`baseline_delete`

Removes one baseline; the tasks are untouched.

`baseline_set_color`

Changes the palette colour of a baseline. Only the colour — the snapshot entries and creation time do not move.

## Two comparisons, not one

Planned-versus-baseline tells you the schedule changed. Actual-versus-baseline tells you the work took longer than promised. They are different facts and they lead to different conversations: the first is usually a scope or dependency decision, the second is an estimate problem.

`kaidoplan baseline create --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan baseline variance --file plan.kaido`

## When to take one

- At the start of each reporting period, so the report has a reference point.

- Before a delivery push, so the promise has a frozen state behind it.

- Before a large re-plan, so the cost of the re-plan is measurable afterwards.

## Immutability is the feature

A snapshot you can edit is a rumour. These entries are frozen at creation, which is why a baseline from three weeks ago still means what it meant then.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I recover an old plan from a baseline?

A baseline records the planned dates at that moment; it is a reference, not a backup. Use the repository or your backup for restoration.

How many baselines can I keep?

They are cheap and listed in creation order. Keep the ones whose comparison you would actually make.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/cli.html

Features · CLI

# The command line

Everything the app can do to the plan, from a terminal — which is also the shortest path to putting a schedule check in CI.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The command surface

`kaidoplan project create|open|save|summary
kaidoplan task add|list|get|update|delete
kaidoplan wbs import
kaidoplan schedule compute|path
kaidoplan violations
kaidoplan status update|batch
kaidoplan resource add|list
kaidoplan baseline create|list|delete|color|variance`

Every command takes `--file`; JSON output is available where a script needs structure rather than formatted text. The CLI works whether or not the app is open — it opens the file, performs the operation and saves.

## The four commands worth memorising

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido # dates from the graph
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido # the chain that sets the date
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido # what the plan admits is broken
kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido # write progress back, per-entry`

## Why a CLI and not only an MCP server

The MCP server needs the app and a client. A shell command needs neither, which makes it the option that survives in scripts, in CI and in a shell history you can read six months later. The two surfaces are the same operations on the same file, so choosing one is not choosing a different feature set.

## Putting it in CI

A dependency cycle can be made a build failure in one line. That is a cheap guarantee: it means no commit can introduce a plan that can never start, and it costs nothing when the check passes.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does the CLI need a licence?

You can use these commands during the free trial. CLI and MCP write operations require an active subscription after the trial.

Can I use it without the app installed?

The CLI is a separate Homebrew package. Whether it needs the app's licence state depends on the operation — reads do not.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/mcp-clients.html

Features · Integration

# Connecting an agent

Five clients, one switch each. The configuration file keeps its formatting, its key order and its other servers.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What the switch does

Turning on a client writes its MCP configuration for you: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy each have a row with a switch. Turning it off removes the same entry. The editor is text-preserving — it adds or removes only `mcpServers.kaidoplan` (for Codex, `[mcp_servers.kaidoplan]`), so indentation, key order and line endings in the rest of the file are untouched.

Each row reports its own state: connected, configuration needs updating, write failed with a reason and a retry, not connected, client not installed. A failure in one client does not affect the others.

## Stdio without a separate install

The app binary can run as a stdio MCP server with `--mcp-stdio`. That mode is intercepted very early in launch: no window, no Dock icon, nothing to close. A client can therefore start the app itself rather than depending on a separately installed CLI.

## The security defaults

- Loopback only — never the LAN, never the internet.

- A bearer token generated locally must accompany every request; it is shown in the panel and can be reset.

- Only folders authorized in the panel are reachable.

- Since v3.4.0 the service is on by default on `127.0.0.1`; an existing explicit off setting is respected rather than overwritten.

## Ports

The first successful bind is persisted, so restarts prefer the same port. If it is taken, the app falls back through a private range of 56 ports without changing the stored preference — so the next launch still tries your port first.

## Try reading and updating a plan

The trial includes both read and write access. After the trial, write-back requires a subscription. The service checks the licence before writing to disk.

## Questions this page does not answer

Do I have to use the switch?

No. A copy-configuration button remains as the manual path for anyone who wants to place the entry themselves.

What happens when the token changes?

Configurations of enabled clients are rewritten automatically, so you do not have to re-paste them.
